newsitem.title: USA: Demand seen tenuous for US Treasury 30-yr auction.
newsitem.headline: Demand seen tenuous for US Treasury 30-yr auction.

text.p: The success of the U.S. Treasury's $10.0 billion auction of 30-year bonds depends partly on whether players think the market is currently fully priced or can make more gains, traders and analysts said.

"I think people are having a little trouble determining whether there's demand right now, given the behavior of the 10-year note," said Steve Ricchuito, chief financial economist at BZW Securities, a primary government securities dealer. "They're starting to wonder whether this thing is just fully priced."
The 30-year bonds to be sold Thursday at 1300 EST/1800 GMT were yielding 6.625 percent in when-issued trade a quarter of an hour before the 1300 EST bidding deadline for the auction.

"It's about a 6-5/8 percent coupon in when-issued trade," said Joseph Benning, a long government trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "It looks like it's going to come in weaker than that -- maybe a 6-3/4 percent coupon and an average yield between 6.63 percent and 6.65 percent."
Benning said the market was under pressure from supply from the Treasury's $38.5 billion refunding operation. Earlier Thursday, the Treasury sold $19.25 billion in year bills.
Another factor affecting demand for the new 30-year bonds is that prices are "at reasonably high levels to begin with," said Benning. "There's not a lot of concession."
The bond market was down sharply in early afternoon trade, hurt by overnight comments of a Japanese finance ministry official and anxiety ahead of the Treasury's 30-year auction.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was down 22/32 to 101-2/32, its yield up to 6.67 percent.

The 10-year notes auctioned on Wednesday as the second part of the Treasury's three-legged quarterly refunding were yielding 6.349 percent in when-issued trade, higher than the average 6.273 percent yield at which they were auctioned.
"The Street doesn't want to buy the paper at current levels," said Ricchuito.

A remark by National Association of Manufacturers president Jerry Jasinowski asserting that he expected the Clinton Administration to de-emphasize its strong dollar policy as the economy slows (without going so far a to talk the dollar down) was also pressuring bonds, Benning said.
"This business of (Treasury Secretary Robert) Rubin planning to de-emphasize a strong dollar hasn't exactly cheered anyone up," said Benning.
Benning noted that "a huge percentage" of buying of U.S. government securities has been by foreigners and "they can't be too happy" if the dollar is suddenly going to weaken.
Still, while Ricchuito said no one foresaw a big book for the 30-year bonds, Benning said the maturity had cheapened up relative to the rest of the yield curve.
"The overall rate is nothing to write home about, but they're reasonably cheap compared to the 10-year sector," said Benning. "There's a yield curve concession."
